title: Why the China-US Naval Encounter at Sabina Shoal Is Different
author: Bao Yinan
text:
The Independence-class littoral combat ship USS Charleston approaches the Wasp-class amphibious assault ship USS Boxer (not pictured) for a fueling-at-sea, Nov. 1, 2025.
Credit: U.S. Navy photo by Mass Communication Specialist 1st Class Daniel Gaither
On October 20, China accused a U.S. naval vessel of “undermining regional stability” by entering waters near Sabina Shoal in the Spratly Islands. According to a spokesperson for the People’s Liberation Army’s Southern Theater Command Navy, the U.S. Littoral Combat Ship USS Charleston (LCS-18) “illegally ​intruded” into waters adjacent to Sabina Shoal “without approval from the Chinese government.” By contrast, a U.S.​ Navy 7th Fleet spokesperson maintained that the Charleston conducted “routine operations in international waters” consistent with international law.This latest naval encounter reflects the long-standing legal dispute between China and the U.S. over the freedom of navigation of warships in the South China Sea. What makes it distinct is the location of the incident: unlike all previous U.S. Freedom of Navigation Operations (FONOPs) targeted at China in the South China Sea, the encounter occurred near Sabina Shoal, a maritime feature not occupied by China. Thus, this is also the first time that the PLA Navy (PLAN) officially admitted that it “dispatched forces to track and monitor the U.S. vessel” near a feature China doesn’t occupy. [...]
